claims.text: A continuous nanometer-scale graphene interlayer can be deposited along the tungsten–copper interface during composite fabrication.
Adding a graphene interlayer at the W–Cu interface will increase the composite's overall thermal conductivity relative to a comparable W–Cu composite without graphene.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to the W–Cu control.
The graphene-enhanced composite will retain resistance to irradiation-induced degradation comparable to the W–Cu control.
The graphene interlayer provides an efficient and robust linkage between tungsten and copper.
The graphene interlayer improves thermal transport across the tungsten–copper interface.
The graphene interlayer facilitates stress transfer across the tungsten–copper interface.
Graphene has extremely high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Graphene's thermal conductivity and strong covalent bonding enhance phonon coupling between tungsten and copper.
Enhanced phonon coupling between tungsten and copper reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Graphene's mechanical strength helps preserve the composite's structural integrity under mechanical loading.
Graphene's radiation tolerance helps preserve the composite's structural integrity during irradiation.
The proposed benefits depend on the graphene layer being defect-free and uniformly integrated.
Excessively thick graphene films or processing damage to the interlayer could negate the proposed improvements.
Irradiation doses or temperatures far beyond the tested regime could compromise graphene's performance.
Direct evidence for the long-term stability of graphene interlayers under high-dose irradiation and high-temperature fusion-reactor conditions is limited.
